claims.claim: The CI `argocd app diff` failures reported in projects that recently enabled the sync impersonation flag are explained by the impersonation design scoping impersonation to the sync path only: the RFC sets Impersonate on the `SyncContext` in the Application Controller's `sync.go` and matches `destinationServiceAccounts` "when executing the kubectl commands for the sync operation", so the server-side-apply dry-run that computes the diff never receives that configuration and runs under a different identity than the sync the reporter is comparing it against.

The unbounded `patch` RBAC escalation on external clusters — five rounds of adding resource kinds to the standing cluster credential's ClusterRole — follows directly from the impersonation RFC's implementation list, which names only the GitOps Engine kubectl sync commands and the Application Controller `sync.go` SyncContext as impersonation touchpoints; because Server-Side Diff issues a server-side apply dry-run that Kubernetes authorizes as `patch` against the cluster Secret credential rather than the AppProject's `defaultServiceAccount`, every new resource kind demands real write authority the design never intended to grant.

The in-cluster CLI diff failure and the external-cluster reconcile failure are two symptoms of one design decision, not two bugs: both report the same `serverSideDiff error: ... is forbidden` string from a server-side apply dry-run, and both occur only where `application.sync.impersonation.enabled` is on, because the RFC applies `destinationServiceAccounts` to the sync operation and leaves the diff identity — `argocd-server` for the CLI path, the cluster Secret credential for the application-controller path — untouched.

The escape from the review-environment permission boundary, where a user commits a `kind: Namespace` matching the AppProject `clusterResourceWhitelist` pattern and drops the `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline` label, is explained by the impersonation RFC's stated granularity decision: "The service account to be used for impersonation is determined on a per Application level rather than on per resource level," using `Application.spec.destination.namespace` for all resources in the Application — so the ticket's proposal to have the Argo CD control plane SA handle namespace bootstrapping while the impersonated SA handles the rest is precisely the per-resource split the design ruled out.

The request to have Argo CD respect users' and groups' existing Kubernetes RBAC instead of duplicating it in Argo CD's own scheme is the case the impersonation RFC deliberately deferred: its design considerations state it is "Not supporting all impersonation options at the moment to keep the initial design to a minimum," with impersonating users or groups left to a future release, and its only configured impersonation subject is `defaultServiceAccount` per destination.

The delete/re-create loop on a manually deleted ApplicationSet child is explained by the deletion PRD's definition of the `Reverse` deletionOrder, which "Waits for one application to be fully deleted before moving onto the next application": a child stuck in Progressing never completes that wait, so the barrier never releases and the controller restarts the wave from the top — a failure mode the PRD does not acknowledge, its Risks and Mitigations section reading "No immediate Risks to consider."

The proposal to run RollingSync steps as `parallel` / `parallelGroups` collides with the deletion PRD's mechanism for `deletionOrder: Reverse`, which is defined as deleting "in the reverse order of the steps configured in RollingSync strategy" and guarded by a check that "can only select reverse if rollingSync lists out an order of application deployment, otherwise should error out" — parallel groups remove the total step order the reverse strategy inverts, so the two features cannot both hold their stated semantics without a rule the PRD does not define.

The reported inability to control destroy order across multiple ApplicationSets — the "shadowed" deletion ordering that forced an app-of-apps-per-cluster workaround to regain sync waves — is the direct consequence of the roadmap's explicit decision that "Deletion of generated Applications is explicitly out of scope for rollout orchestration," with teardown left as a manual operator action performed one Application at a time.

Asking for Source Hydrator support on ApplicationSets runs into the hydrator RFC's placement decision: `sourceHydrator` is an Application `spec` field, mutually exclusive with `source` and `sources`, and hydration is driven by grouping existing Applications by `drySource` repo/targetRevision and then by `syncSource.targetBranch` — there is no generator-level hydration stage, so the ticket's `appset-of-apps` shape that hydrates generated Applications into a Git repo has no field to hang off in the current design.

The hydrator pilot repository's per-push wave behavior in the ProgressiveSync bug is explained by the hydrator RFC's commit model: "Changes originating from a single dry commit are always grouped into a single hydrated commit" on `syncSource.targetBranch`, and "When the application controller detects a new (hydrated) commit on the `syncSource.targetBranch`, it will sync the manifests" — so on a hydrated repo every hydration cycle presents a fresh source change to RollingSync, which is why the pilot is the environment where the spec-only trigger loss surfaces.

Auto-sync deploying stale manifests after a hydrator sync-source change is the expected behavior of the hydrator RFC's push-to-stage mode, in which manifests go to the optional `hydrateTo.targetBranch` and "Argo CD relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch" — the deployment branch therefore still holds whatever the promoter last moved, which is exactly the condition the ticket reports observing only in push-to-stage.

The commit server pushing unsigned hydrated commits, so that Argo CD rejects its own hydrated output when signature verification is enabled on the hydrated branch, traces to the hydrator RFC's Push access design, which specifies only a `repository-write` Kubernetes Secret carrying GitHub App credentials for the delegated push and raises no signing requirement — its Security Considerations name push permissions, branch protection, and secret placement, never commit signatures.

The missing `Chart` field on DrySource, and the resulting forced move to Helm dependencies, is the hydrator RFC's stated design: `spec.sourceHydrator.drySource` "contains only three fields: `repoURL`, `targetRevision`, and `path`," and the RFC explicitly drops multi-source support in favor of "the umbrella chart approach," accepting the loss of convenience — which is the same umbrella-chart cost the ticket reports as blocking chart-version control across environments via ApplicationSets.

The rollback proposal to have Rollback write `git checkout $rollback_revision -- $sync_path` directly to the sync branch in both hydrator modes cuts across the hydrator RFC's push-to-stage contract, where the `hydrateTo` branch exists so a commit can be staged before deployment and an external promotion system owns the move into `syncSource.targetBranch`; a rollback commit that bypasses the staging branch enters the deployment branch outside the promoter's lineage, which is why the ticket has to add commit metadata "for any promotion system to later make a decision on whether it is safe to promote new commits."

The auto-sync skip that requires "a new commit B must arrive while the application is still syncing to commit A" is a rare race under hand-authored branches but a steady state under the hydrator RFC, which has the controller push a hydrated commit to `syncSource.targetBranch` for every dry commit and sync on detecting it — so hydrated branches turn the reported `Status.Sync.Revision` versus actual synced revision defect from an edge case into a recurring one wherever `manifest-generate-paths` is set without `selfHeal`.
